Neisse
NY-suh
n. (the Silesian town of the prince-bishops of Breslau, from which the Catholic Reformation was pressed on a largely Lutheran duchy)
From the river Neisse, a Slavic hydronym; the Polish form is Nysa.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Neisse in Silesia was the chief town of the duchy held by the prince-bishops of Breslau and so a Catholic island in a province that had gone overwhelmingly Lutheran in the fifteen-twenties. From the later sixteenth century it was the base of the Catholic recovery in Silesia: a Jesuit college was founded in 1622, and after the Habsburg victory over the Bohemian Protestants the churches of the duchy and of the crown lands were taken back, Lutheran ministers expelled, and conformity pressed by commissions, with the Peace of Westphalia securing only three plain timber churches of peace for the whole province. Frederick the Great's conquest of Silesia in 1740 reversed the position again. The dictionary records Neisse because Silesia is the best-documented example of a province changed by administration twice within a century, and because the churches of peace, built of wood outside the walls and holding thousands, are the plainest monument in Europe to a people who would not stop assembling.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines conformity as compliance with an established form; a commission as a body of persons authorised to act; an assembly as a company met together; timber as wood for building; and constancy as firmness of mind.

expand to see more

CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence with a model or pattern; compliance with the usages of the established church.

COMMISSION, n. A number of persons joined in an office or trust; the warrant by which authority is conferred.

ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, usually for some common purpose.

TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture and the like.

CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; firmness of mind; steadiness; perseverance in a purpose or opinion.

Key Scripture

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Act 2:46 — "And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,"

Mat 18:20 — "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."

Act 5:42 — "And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ."

Modern Corruption

Silesian town of the prince-bishops of Breslau, base of the Catholic recovery that took back the province's churches and left Protestants three timber churches of peace.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the use of commissions, registers and the confiscation of buildings to reverse a people's religion, which Silesia suffered twice. The dictionary notes what the Silesian Lutherans did when their churches were taken, which was to go on meeting: at the border, in the woods, and finally in three enormous timber barns built outside town walls by permission of a treaty. The command they were obeying is explicit and is given against a known tendency: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the church is a gathering and not a building. Christ fixes the minimum and attaches himself to it, “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20); the first church met in both large and small places, “daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house” (Act 2:46); and when forbidden the apostles simply continued, for “daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42). Taking a congregation's roof is a serious injury and it is not a solution.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together; Greek oikos (G3624), a house; Greek sunago (G4863), to gather.

expand to see more

Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together, an assembling; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together”, Hebrews 10:25.

Greek sunago (G4863) — to gather together, to assemble; “where two or three are gathered together in my name”, Matthew 18:20.

Greek oikos (G3624) — a house, a household; “and breaking bread from house to house”, Acts 2:46.

Greek pauo (G3973) — to cease, to stop; “they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ”, Acts 5:42.

Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to announce good news; “to teach and preach Jesus Christ”, Acts 5:42.

Usage

"“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — the command the Silesians obeyed in barns."

"“where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — the minimum, with a promise attached."

"“they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42) — the apostolic response to a prohibition."
